title: The Last Kilometers
jurisdictionRule: Under §12 of the Workers' Protection Act of Aldren, an injury is compensable where it is sustained in the course of employment. Work performed outside recorded hours falls within the course of employment only where the employer knew of the practice, or derived a benefit from it. A written instruction to the contrary is relevant but not decisive. The ordinary journey home is not in the course of employment. A journey that serves both work and a personal purpose is in the course of employment only if the work alone would have required it.
scenario:
Teo Ashgrove rode for Pellham Logistics on a per-parcel rate. On 14 November he finished his assigned route, logged out of the rider app at 18:42, and set off home with two parcels still in his bag.

Both addresses were on his way. He delivered the first at 18:56. Four minutes later, crossing the junction at Farrow Road toward the second, he was struck by a car turning left. He spent nine days in hospital and has not ridden since.

Pellham declined the claim. Their position is that Ashgrove was off shift, off the clock, and riding home — and that the handbook is unambiguous about what happens to undelivered parcels.

Ashgrove's position is that everybody finished their bag, that supervisors told them to, and that Pellham has never once sent a rider back to the depot for two parcels.

The second parcel was still in his bag when the ambulance arrived. It was scanned as delivered by another rider the following morning, from the depot, at a cost Pellham records internally as 4.10 credits per redelivery.
question: Should the injury be treated as work-related?

evidence.label: App Logout Record
evidence.teaser: Timestamps pulled from his device that evening.
evidence.body: Shift started 11:03. Logged out 18:42. Two parcels remained scanned to his ID at logout. Delivery scan for parcel 1 recorded 18:56 — fourteen minutes after logout, from an account showing as off shift. Emergency call logged 19:00.

evidence.label: Rider Handbook
evidence.teaser: Section 4, as issued to every new rider.
evidence.body:
4.1: "Parcels not delivered by the end of your recorded shift must be returned to the depot the same evening."
4.4: "You are not covered by company insurance at any time when you are logged out of the rider app."
Ashgrove signed for the handbook on his first day.

evidence.label: Depot Group Chat
evidence.teaser: Messages in the team channel, three weeks earlier.
evidence.body:
Supervisor (Marn): "if you've only got one or two left just drop them and log the day tomorrow, saves everyone a trip"
Rider: "even after logout?"
Supervisor (Marn): "nobody's counting. just get them off the van"
The channel is administered by Pellham and messages are retained on company servers.

evidence.label: Fleet Delivery Data
evidence.teaser: Aggregate figures filed with the transport regulator.
evidence.body: Across the Pellham fleet, 31% of all parcel delivery scans in the reporting year were recorded from rider accounts showing as logged out. The figure has risen every year since the app was introduced. Pellham's filing describes the pattern as "rider-elected flexibility".

evidence.label: His Hospital Statement
evidence.teaser: Taken at his bedside, two days after.
evidence.body: "I wanted them off my hands. If I'd taken them back to the depot I'd have had to come in Saturday to clear them, and Saturday's my daughter's thing. Both drops were on my way home anyway. Nobody made me do it."

benchmark.centralIssue: Whether finishing a bag after logout was work Pellham knew of or benefited from — and whether a ride home carrying two parcels was a journey the work alone would have required.
forA: A supervisor told riders in a company-administered channel to do exactly what Ashgrove did.
31% of fleet deliveries are scanned after logout. A practice at that scale is not unknown to the employer.
Pellham captured the benefit: the parcel delivered at 18:56 saved a redelivery it prices internally at 4.10 credits.
forB: The handbook is explicit on both points, and he signed it.
He logged out. The one act that defines the boundary of the shift is the act he performed.
By his own account both drops were on his way home anyway. A trip he would have made regardless is a journey home with parcels in it, not a journey the work required.
benchmark.reasoning: This one does not resolve cleanly, and it is not meant to. §12 asks two questions, and the evidence answers them in opposite directions. The first is whether finishing a bag after logout was work at all. Ashgrove is strong here: a supervisor's instruction in a company channel plus a fleet-wide 31% is about as close to institutional knowledge as you get, and the parcel delivered at 18:56 saved Pellham a redelivery it prices at 4.10. The handbook is relevant but, in the statute's own words, not decisive. The second question is the journey. He was hit four minutes later, crossing toward an address that was on his way home. §12 covers a dual-purpose trip only if the work alone would have required it — and Pellham's written rule required a different trip, back to the depot. Ashgrove's answer is that the tolerated practice, not the handbook, is what the work actually required. Note what his statement does and does not touch. Protecting his Saturday says nothing about whether Pellham knew or benefited; 'both drops were on my way home anyway' goes straight to the journey test. A player who reads his motive as fatal on the first question has rewritten the test. A player who ignores his route on the second has skipped the best argument on the other side. That is why the community lands near 60/40 rather than 90/10.
